items.body: Review by ProgExpert — It is amazing to hear H�llas go fully prog on *Panorama*. The record feels broader, more ambitious, and more mature than ever, while still retaining the melodic instinct and personality that make the band distinctive. I only wish a few especially beautiful musical ideas had been explored further, particularly the passage around 3:30 in the first suite and the wonderful final theme at the very end of the last song. Those moments are so strong that I wanted them to keep unfolding. It is brilliant to hear these artists growing in ambition and maturity. We simply cannot have enough of this music.

items.body: Review by ProgExpert — This is a remarkably delicate and sensitive record, played with exceptional taste throughout. Every arrangement feels carefully judged... nothing is overstated, and the musicianship is consistently impressive without ever becoming showy. There is a warmth and naturalness to the playing that gives the music an almost timeless quality! At several moments, it recalls the more pastoral and adventurous side of 1970s Caravan, with that same combination of melodic richness, subtle complexity, and effortless flow. What stands out most, though, is the restraint. Beautifully performed, elegant, and deeply musical. I cannot get enough, I wish they had composed 10 records! Not just 2! Come back Jouis!

items.body: Review by ValeriyK — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeOMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time continues the story started with OMNI, released by Antony Kalugin in 2025. And, without any doubt, OMNI II is one of the brightest progressive rock releases of 2026.A wonderful cast of musicians, clear and rich production and, most importantly, strong melodies make OMNI II a very enjoyable album from beginning to end. There is a lot of good music here, and I have already returned to this album many times.Like the previous OMNI, the music is divided into larger chapters. Here we have OMNI Part 4, Part 5 and the bonus Part 6, each approximately the length of one vinyl side.OMNI Part 4The album opens with The Glass of Time Part 1, and what a pleasure it is to hear Rob Reed here. For almost the first minute and forty seconds, it is basically Rob's world: keyboards, guitars and bass. Then Michel St-P�re and Antony Kalugin join in and the piece develops into a wonderful instrumental with a strong classic Genesis and Tony Banks flavour. It is a beautiful and very natural opening to the album.The second track, Frozen Rivers, is without doubt one of the highlights of the album. Here we meet the wizard Roine Stolt, one of the finest composers and guitarists in modern progressive rock, together with his brother Michael Stolt on bass. There is a very strong Scandinavian feeling running through this composition. Kalugin has mentioned that he wrote this song especially for Roine, and even the lyrics seem to reflect that connection.It is also a pleasure to hear John Hackett again on flute and Marek Arnold on soprano saxophone. Everything comes together beautifully, and the lyrics have a warm and soulful quality. For me, this is one of those tracks that immediately makes you want to press repeat.Then comes Shadowbound, and this is simply a hit. In another musical universe I could easily imagine this song appearing at Eurovision and doing very well there. It has an immediate melody and a memorable chorus, but underneath that accessible surface there is still plenty happening.The song deals with destiny, our choices and the struggle between different sides of ourselves. Mariya Panasenko is the real star here. Her performance is powerful, emotional and technically excellent, while Jannica Lund adds beautiful backing vocals and Roine Stolt contributes guitar. In the middle the song suddenly opens into a symphonic art-rock section. Somehow Karfagen manages to put Eurovision and progressive rock into the same four minutes ? and it works!Part 4 closes with The Shape of Love, featuring Marco Gl�hmann of Sylvan. Marco is surely one of the most distinctive vocalists in contemporary progressive rock. His voice is immediately recognisable, and the emotional range he brings to a song is remarkable.Just as The Last Card was one of my favourite moments on the first OMNI, The Shape of Love is one of the strongest songs here. It is also nice to hear Kalugin writing so openly about love again. I sincerely hope Marco will return for the next chapter of OMNI, because his voice brings so much emotion to this music.OMNI Part 5Part 5 begins with the nine-minute Carry On, and my only complaint is that I wish it were even longer!This is warm, vintage progressive rock, somewhere in the world of Alan Parsons and Electric Light Orchestra, but still unmistakably Karfagen. Yogi Lang of RPWL provides his characteristic vocals, and the composition develops through two rather different moods. The first section is energetic, positive, almost feel-good prog, while the second becomes more balladic and has, to my ears, something of the spirit of classic ELO.Kalle Wallner, also well known from RPWL and Blind Ego, appears on guitar, and it is great to see these two Bavarian musicians together on a Karfagen album. Michael Stolt once again provides his strong and dependable bass work.Beyond the Mirror brings back Per Malmberg, whom listeners of the first OMNI may remember from The Spark. Pascal Gutman adds Chapman Stick, and the result is another melodic and very positive song.And finally we hear Antony himself singing a verse! One thing I noticed on this album is that there is actually not very much lead vocal from Kalugin. Of course this is his artistic decision, but personally I enjoy his voice and hope to hear more of it on future albums.There is also a lovely moment in the middle of Beyond the Mirror where Jannica Lund's backing vocals meet acoustic guitar. Believe it or not, it reminds me of Fleetwood Mac ? that old, warm, soft pop-rock feeling ? and it fits surprisingly well.How Fragile We Are is a charming, enveloping and very gentle ballad. Mariya Panasenko sings beautifully, while Marek Arnold's soprano saxophone almost answers her voice like a second singer in a duet. Antony can also be heard on backing vocals in the chorus.There is something very Gilmour-like and Pink Floyd-like about the atmosphere here. Nothing is rushed. The song simply breathes, until we are left with the words: "Oh, how fragile we are?"The main album then closes with The Glass of Time Part 2, bringing us back to Rob Reed. Once again, for roughly the opening minute and forty seconds, Rob carries almost everything himself ? keyboards, guitar and bass. :)It works like a mirror of The Glass of Time Part 1, bringing the main album full circle. This is Karfagen instrumental music in its natural territory, with another gentle touch of Genesis and Tony Banks. A wonderful ending to the main 48-minute album.But fortunately, the CD does not stop there.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent CompassInstead of releasing another separate Working Tapes disc this time, Kalugin has included the complete OMNI Part 6, lasting just over nineteen minutes, as a bonus chapter on the CD. This material has also been announced as a separate digital release titled The Silent Compass, coming to streaming platforms this Friday. But CD listeners receive the whole additional chapter together with the main album. Thank you, Antony!It begins with Under the Northern Lights, a tiny piece lasting less than two minutes, but what a beautiful two minutes they are. This is almost classical music: piano, organ and orchestral colours, soprano saxophone, Roine Stolt's guitar and John Hackett's flute. There is something of Edvard Grieg in its atmosphere, perfectly matching the northern mood suggested by the title. A miniature symphonic pleasure.Then we arrive at The Silent Compass, one of the finest instrumentals on the whole release. Roine Stolt and Roberto D�az of Anima Mundi create a wonderful dialogue between their guitars. Max Velychko provides excellent acoustic guitar and John Hackett opens the piece beautifully on flute.There are shades of Anthony Phillips and The Flower Kings here, but ultimately this is Karfagen doing what Karfagen does best: melodic, pastoral and symphonic progressive rock with plenty of space for the musicians to tell their own stories.OM

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Really 4.75, but clicked 5...4 is too low.Quivira are new prog band consisting of: ?Jake Livgren (Emerald City Council, Kerry Livgren Band, Proto Kaw?he's Kerry's nephew) on lead vocals, ?Composer Lisa LaRue (RematriNation, Solo, 2KX, Federico Fantacone), on keyboards and programming, and ?John Baker (Forever Twelve, Mars Hollow, Little Girls) on guitars, bass and vocals. There are two guest performers: - Joe Deninzon (Kansas, Stratospheerius) / violin (5)- Evan Stanley (Stanley-Simmons?Paul Stanley's son) / guitar (9)According to the press release:This project blends historical themes, classic rock, and cinematic progressive rock into multi-movement works that emphasize narrative cohesion, harmonic exploration, and textural depth. The debut focuses on the story of pre-Kansas "Quivira", the Native American villages that Coronado believed held gold.This album comes courtesy of Nick Katona of Melodic Revolution Records (MRR). As always, I receive no further compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Track 1 - (Intro) The Coming of the Spaniards (3:52)A blend of vocal and string sounds provides a cinematic beginning, joined by drum accents. This feels like the beginning of an epic movie. Acoustic guitar gradually enters the soundscape along with the choral and orchestral themes. The acoustic guitar becomes more prominent as we proceed. A grand introduction!Track 2 - The Benefits of Breathing Quietly (5:55)The music quiets down to a single violin-like sound, then piano, bass and percussion enter. Jake Livgren enters on vocals with a very expressive melody. There are wonderful harmonies as the verse continues to build. The piano parts are absolutely beautiful as a synth solo enters soon after. The sound is warm and full; great production. Jake's vocals are exceptional! Not to play too heavily on the Kansas connection, but he is reminiscent of Steve Walsh in his prime. Lisa LaRue's synth solo is fantastic. The drum programming has some nice fills and syncs nicely, but I would always prefer a live drummer. Outstanding piano work as the song nears its conclusion. Jake closes it out with more top-notch vocals. Fantastic track!Track 3 - The Plains Truth (6:49)A quiet piano starts things off here. I believe the violin is synthesized, but it's convincing. This album is very dynamic! We get into a nice 6-8 groove here. John Baker has a nice guitar solo, making good use of delay effects. This is a wonderful instrumental track! Baker plays an acoustic solo at around 5:45 as well. Lisa LaRue shows her strengths here, not only as a terrific keyboardist, but an amazing composer and arranger. Another great piece of music! Track 4 - Quivira Bound (5:31)This begins with a prog-tastic intro with the synth in the spotlight, followed by acoustic guitar. Jake returns on vocals at around the 40 second point. I love the accents and harmonies as it approaches the chorus. This is glorious! The synth fill before the second verse is outstanding. Again, I hate to compare too much, but this really does remind me of classic Kansas. The "violin" solo could be Robbie Steinhardt. A strong guitar solo from Baker follows. I'm loving this track!Track 5 - Moving Forward (6:49)This commences with a brisk 6-8 and moves through several odd meters. This is the track on which current Kansas violinist Joe Deninzon appears, and his presence is felt early. This track will appeal to fans of prog with lots of meter changes. Joe's violin sounds like it's being fed through a distortion pedal, and even a wah-wah at times. Baker has a super-cool guitar feature after that. LaRue's piano continues to impress. Even the drum machine parts are solid and fit perfectly. This is another instrumental-only track, and it's amazing! Track 6 - The Turk - Follow the Wind (5:37)A syncopated piano part starts us off here. The vocals have adopted an accent, presumably that of "The Turk". A drum-groove and bass enter at around 1:25 to help propel the momentum. Nice change of pace into the chorus. The "violin" parts sound so realistic, I'm surprised it's not Joe Deninzon throughout the album. The solo that closes out the track is evidence of that. There are some sound effects at the tail end. This is another spectacular song!Track 7 - Nothing Is Everything (7:31)This one gets going with a high energy intro not unlike "No One Together". Again, I apologize, but this REALLY sounds like classic Kansas, while still being original?maybe it's just the setting of the music, but it really evokes that vibe. The intro consumes the first 3-minutes of the track, but I doubt anyone will mind! That was incredible! Things quiet down and become calm following the intro. There is a slow-build beginning at 3:45. I think this is another instrumental. Again, the dynamics on this album are incredible! LaRue's piano at 5:45 is nothing short of masterful. An acoustic guitar solo follows. Another stunningly awesome piece of music!Track 8 - Carved From the Sun (8:01) A mid-tempo introduction starts off this longest track. I like the bass line. The musicians have layered beautiful melodies and harmonies over the rhythm section. The tempo picks up at 1:40. This one rocks hard! Yet, that's not all it does. The arrangements throughout this album have been impressive; every bit is right where it should be. I think Jake is sitting this one out, too. Lisa and John have crafted some amazing instrumental prog here. Track 9 - Kicking Rocks (4:18)This is the track on which Evan Stanley plays. I have to say that when I learned that KISS' Paul Stanley's son was playing on this, I didn't see THAT coming! Piano and bass open the track, and the drums soon enter. Great bass line from John Baker. Evan Stanley's guitar playing is excellent. He and LaRue alternate between guitar and piano breaks. I like the blend of piano and synth. Stanley's main feature seems to be at around 3:00, and it's quite good. Track 10 - Prelude to Anywhere - Weekend Conquistadors (5:42)LaRue's fluid piano lines bring us into this track. After a cinematic opening, some short guitar riffs tease us. More masterful playing from LaRue follows. Hey, Jake's back at 2:40. He's accompanied by piano only at first, then the rest of the "band" kicks in for the chorus. And it's a great chorus at that! I love the lull then crescendo with about a minute left. Things quiet down, then there are spoken words:Male voice: "I will go to the end of the earth for that which I seek."Female voice: "True gain in life is not measured by the things we accumulate, but by the peace we possess."Awesome track!Track 11 - Still Breathing (5:58)Beautiful piano and violin take us into the final song. At around 40 seconds, big accents help amp up the energy. At 1:15, the music temporarily pauses. Shortly afterward, the beat kicks in for some wonderful melodies. I believe this is another instrumental track to close out this fabulous album. Tempo and mood changes abound! This one is quite cinematic as well. As the track fades out a horse neighs and trots off. A terrific ending!OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:I keep having to say what an amazing year this has been for prog rock! I thought 2025 was great, which it was, but this year is phenomenal! Quivira have entered the running for prog album of the year here as well! What a debut! Certainly, a contender for best new prog band! My only nit-pick is that I would have preferred a live drummer. That said, the drum machine programming is very well-done. Lisa LaRue has established herself as a premiere composer, arranger and keyboardist. I am blown away. I was already familiar with Jake from his work with his uncle and even more so with Emerald City Council, but he really knocked me out with his performances on this album; spectacular. John Baker's bass parts and, especially his acoustic solos are quite tasty. I give this a nearly perfect 4.75 out of 5 stars (95%). Fans of symphonic classic prog will love the hell out of this album!

items.body: Review by Abrasmatheus — Masterpiece from a band at the height of its creativityI have known A Night at the Opera since my teenage years, when it became one of my favorite albums. I first heard it through my father during family road trips, and those memories are certainly one of the reasons why this album remains so special to me. The fact that I did not approach it with any particular expectations and simply discovered it naturally makes my relationship with the record even more personal.For me, A Night at the Opera is one of Queen's best albums. It is remarkably consistent, with no weak tracks, and it perfectly represents many of the elements that made the band so distinctive during the 1970s. Hard rock, rock opera, pop, folk influences and theatrical arrangements are all present here, creating an extremely varied but cohesive album.I would not call A Night at the Opera a progressive rock album, but it undoubtedly contains several progressive elements. The clearest example is 'The Prophet's Song', probably the most progressive composition on the record. Its unusual structure, extended length, dramatic changes in atmosphere, complex vocal sections and ambitious arrangements give it a much more progressive character than the rest of the album. The famous vocal canon in the middle of the song, with multiple overlapping voices creating an almost hypnotic effect, is particularly impressive. The track also develops through different sections rather than following a simple verse-chorus format, making it one of the most adventurous compositions Queen ever recorded.The album's production and arrangements are also among its greatest strengths. Even without being an expert in production, it is impossible not to notice the enormous amount of detail in the record. The layered vocal harmonies, guitar overdubs, theatrical arrangements and constant stylistic changes create a rich and almost cinematic sound. This is an album that rewards repeated listening because there always seems to be some new detail to discover.Freddie Mercury delivers some absolutely beautiful vocal performances throughout the album. In my opinion, he had the greatest voice in rock music, and A Night at the Opera offers plenty of evidence for that opinion. Brian May's voice on ''39' is also a highlight, perfectly fitting the song's folk rock atmosphere, while Roger Taylor's more aggressive vocals make 'I'm in Love with My Car' a strong hard rock track.The album opens brilliantly with 'Death on Two Legs', an aggressive combination of hard rock and theatricality that immediately displays one of Queen's greatest identities during the 1970s. 'Lazing on a Sunday Afternoon' is one of the most unusual songs on the album and has a very distinctive character, while 'I'm in Love with My Car' brings a more direct hard rock approach and is also a perfect song for a road trip.'You're My Best Friend' is another extremely memorable track, while ''39' is one of my personal favorites because of its wonderful folk rock character and Brian May's vocals. 'Sweet Lady' brings another excellent dose of Queen's hard rock side, while 'Love of My Life' is probably one of the more pop-oriented songs on the album and became one of Queen's most iconic compositions.'Good Company' is another fascinating and unusual track, difficult to place stylistically but similar in spirit to 'Lazing on a Sunday Afternoon' in its old-fashioned and theatrical approach.And then there is 'Bohemian Rhapsody'.For me, this is not only the best song on the album but the greatest rock song of all time. It deserves every bit of its legendary reputation. The combination of ballad, opera and hard rock was an extraordinary innovation, and the composition remains as impressive today as it was when the album was released. It is a true rock anthem, but its fame should not overshadow the fact that the song is also an incredibly ambitious piece of musical creativity.The transition from 'The Prophet's Song' into 'Love of My Life' is another of my favorite moments on the album. Although the two songs are completely different, their placement creates a memorable contrast and contributes to the album's dramatic flow.No track is weak here. Every song has its own identity, and the diversity of styles never makes the album feel unfocused. If anything, that diversity is one of its greatest strengths.In my opinion, A Night at the Opera stands alongside Queen, Queen II, Sheer Heart Attack and A Day at the Races as one of the best albums Queen ever made. It may not be a progressive rock album in the strict sense, but its ambitious compositions and willingness to experiment with different musical styles explain why it can appeal strongly to progressive rock listeners.More importantly, this is an album I associate with family road trips and my adolescence, which makes it personally significant to me. However, even putting nostalgia aside, I still consider it an outstanding record that deserves its legendary status.Recommended to every fan of classic rock.

items.body: Review by Trinity S — Karfagen ? OMNI II Act I: The Glass of TimeI recently received the new OMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time CD directly from Antony Kalugin and, after several listens, I would like to share a few impressions.First of all, this album sounds great. The production, mixing and mastering are excellent: clear, warm and dynamic, with enough space for all the keyboards, guitars, flute, saxophone and vocals. I especially enjoyed listening to it on headphones, where many small details become more noticeable.A special mention should go to Aleksandr Murenko on drums. With so many well-known guests on the album, his contribution could easily be overlooked, but his playing is powerful, musical and very tasteful throughout.The list of guests is impressive, but fortunately the album never feels like a collection of separate performances. Musicians such as Roine and Michael Stolt, Rob Reed, John Hackett, Marco Gl�hmann, Yogi Lang, Kalle Wallner, Michel St-P�re and Marek Arnold all become part of the same musical world.And this really does feel like a world. The beautiful artwork, booklet and posters look almost like a map from a Tolkien fantasy universe. Together with the different singers, instrumental passages and recurring musical themes, OMNI II sometimes feels like a progressive rock opera.Among my personal highlights are Frozen Rivers, with its wonderful Scandinavian atmosphere and Roine Stolt's guitar, the beautiful The Shape of Love with Marco Gl�hmann, and the nine-minute Carry On featuring Yogi Lang and Kalle Wallner.OMNI Part 6 ? The Silent Compass may be presented as an additional part of the CD, but to my ears this is absolutely not bonus or leftover material. It is a strong and complete chapter in its own right. I especially enjoyed the instrumental The Silent Compass, with its beautiful guitar dialogue and John Hackett's flute, and We Live While We Remember, a wonderful and emotional ballad featuring Jean Pageau. These are actually among my favourite moments on the whole release.There was another nice surprise in my package: The Spektral World of Prog ? Volume 2 sampler CD. It was a pleasure to hear some familiar names alongside bands and tracks that were completely new to me. Thanks to Antony for making these companion releases ? they are a nice extra for those who still enjoy buying physical music.Beautiful presentation, excellent sound, strong compositions and first-class musicianship. OMNI II Act I: The Glass of Time is another very strong Karfagen album and one I will certainly return to.Five stars. Rock on!

items.body: Review by alainPP — 1. "Two Roads": for the prog intro?100% spot-on?with crystalline guitar work washing over the ears and Anna's divine vocals (defying her age) channeling the style of the great Kate Bush. The atmosphere is inimitable and highly accessible, featuring Floyd-esque guitar work reminiscent of a sensitive Gary Moore, alongside flute and keyboards that evoke?however distantly?the renowned band Collage. In short, a heavyweight track in the neo-prog scene!2. "Shadows in the Dark": for the breakdown and the warm vocals of Marcin (the singer, not the guitarist); for the solemn, delicate finale featuring a melting piano and a spellbinding choir, with keyboard tones that echo the soundscapes of Vangelis.3. "Single Game": for a vibrant, colorful ballad featuring soaring, moving vocals; it shifts into an atmospheric, classical mode driven by lush keyboards, leading into a beautiful decrescendo.4. "Cheaters": featuring an intro with an electro-new-wave vibe; for the tension and the soaring guitar solo that drives this energetic track, along with a sharp riff reminiscent of Saga?in short, it's punchy and infectious. Prog is right here before you.5. "When We Played By Heart": for the return of Anna?who remains, in my view, the highlight of this album?with vocals that drift seamlessly across prog, atmospheric, and ambient spaces. Her contributions to numerous Polish bands often elevate the quality of their albums. Special mention goes to the bewitching violin that pairs perfectly with this vibrant ballad.6. "Silent Rooms": for the piano interlude showcasing Kamil's magical, fiery touch; his keyboards convey far more emotion than those of many better-known neo-prog players?which says a lot. A beautiful opening to launch...7. "Friends of Blood": featuring a guitar solo by Marcin?a top-tier guest musician. It's an accessible track; the album needed something more repetitive and melodic that truly takes flight with that stratospheric solo. ...a finale that makes you want to hit replay.8. "All About You" begins with a syrupy, Floyd-esque intro; Anna seamlessly joins in, lending this soft, melodic track a sense of tenderness and voluptuousness?indeed, a highly sexualized feel. The melody builds, exploding in hushed tones?the price paid for such musical ecstasy. It is a multi-layered track that settles into the violin before launching back into Anna's compulsive, punky, trance-like mantra as the sound unfolds. Ideal for an endless finale. (4.25)

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — For this ambitious recording of original compositions--which were dedicated to "the two immortals who produced the greatest orchestral jazz music," Duke Ellington and Gil Evans--Neil resuscitated the old New Jazz Orchestra that he had directed and help found back in the early 1960s with Jon Hiseman and Tony Reeves (as well as Jack Bruce, Dick Heckstall-Smith, and Ian Carr and Henry Lowther). The music was recorded sometime in 1971 but it was not released to the public until sometime in 1972, probably early. The list of musicians is a veritable Who's Who of British Jazz Rock.A. "A Symphony of Amaranths" (24:59) a seriously classical composition and production with some jazzy elements but more of an Impressionist/Expressionist type of cinematic music. Absolutely, stunningly beautiful! Without hesitation I must say that this composition alone does tremendous justice to the two heroes to which he dedicated it. I find no flaw; correction: I find myself too small to even possibly due justice to any critique or criticism to this amazing piece of music. I wouldn't change a single note it feels so perfect, feeds my soul so completely. (50/50) - "Carillon" - "Nocturne" - "Entracte" - "Improptu"B1. "The Dong With a Luminous Nose" (11:50) narrator Ivor Cutler recites the words of Edward Lear over Neil's wonderfully fitting jazz-infused orchestra soundtrack. (22.875/25)"Three Poems": Norma Winstone sings the poetry lyrics of W.B. Yeats, James Joyce, and Lewis Carroll, respectively, during the following three musical renderings of Neil's own musical interpretations. Norma was fresh off of being voted by Melody Maker magazine as the top female Jazz Singer of 1971 (which makes this quite the coup for Neil). B2. "After Long Silence" (4:09) Norma Winstone has an incredible voice: one that I would follow to the ends of the Earth. Her voice reminds me of the upbeat, positive tones of both Swing Out Sister's Corinne Drewery and No Small Affair's Demi Moore performance of "My Funny Valentine" as dubbed by Chrissie Faith. (10/10)B3. "She Weeps Over Rahoon" (3:22) Norma, again, but this time singing a very different style: here sounding like a fuller voiced, whisper-toned version of the great modern avant prog singer Elaine di Falco (Thinking Plague, Francesco Zago projects for Fading Records/AltrOck Productions in the 2010s). (9.125/10)B4. "Will You Walk a Little Faster?" (3:48) opening with some upper register scatting � la Ella or Urszula Dudziak, but once the song gets into full swing (pun intended) it's a showtune tour de force/extravaganza. Ver ysimilar to the skill level and stylings of Barbra Streisand's Broadway career and previewing the type of sounds and skills we'll soon be hearing from Renaissance's Annie Haslam. (9.25/10) Total time: 48:08A zesty tongue-in-cheek version of the UK national anthem ends the album, but we don't need to count that (as fun as it was to hear everyone in the studio's control room cracking up at the end).Neal was one of those incredibly gifted and talented humans whose artistic abilities almost require one to drop the mantle of "Renaissance Man" on his shoulders. What a loss to the music world it was that his career in the writing and publishing world spawned such a lucrative and demanding life for him. (Author of Britain's World Book Encyclopedia and founding member of the Dorling Kindersley [DK] "How Things Work" series of children's books--all of which led to sales in the multiples of millions.) Each of his symphonic, choral, and New Jazz Orchestra projects could have generated equal fame and, hopefully, fortune. But here we are.A/five stars; a masterpiece of music no matter what kind you want to call it. I am so glad to have discovered this amazing album; I will cherish FOREVER!

items.body: Cabaret Voltaire have released the 7-inch version of “Don’t Argue”, the second track lifted from the remastered reissue of their 1987 album “CODE”, out 9 October on Mute. The Sheffield electronic duo’s original recording was produced by Cabaret Voltaire with Adrian Sherwood and built around vocal samples from Frank Capra’s 1945 short film “Your Job In Germany”. It reached the UK Singles Chart on its original release. The track follows the John Robie dub mix of “Thank You America”, shared in July when Mute announced the remastered “CODE” reissue. Out of print for years, the album returns on limited edition “CODIFIED” marble vinyl and as a triple CD set, the latter adding two discs of remastered period remixes plus unreleased mixes found in the archive. Both editions carry new sleeve notes on the album’s production and its afterlife. The 7-inch version of “Don’t Argue” sits on disc two, alongside the Hate and Destroy Mix and the single mix of the same track. “CODE” was recorded at the band’s Western Works studio in Sheffield, with Sherwood joining for pre-production before sessions moved to Red Bus in London for mixing. Guest players include saxophonist Simeon Lister, bassist Mark Brydon of Chakk and Bill Nelson of Be-Bop Deluxe. Denis Blackman handled the remaster; work on the reissue began in 2019 with Richard H. Kirk and was completed after his death using his notes, in consultation with Stephen Mallinder and Kirk’s estate. Cabaret Voltaire tour dates in 2026 Stephen Mallinder and Chris Watson close the run they began in 2025 for the 50th anniversary of the band’s first performance. I Speak Machine supports the North American leg, Gazelle Twin most of the UK dates and Fader the two Welsh and south-west English shows. 11 September – Dallas, TX (US), Granada Theater, with I Speak Machine 15 September – Chicago, IL (US), Metro, with I Speak Machine 16 September – Chicago, IL (US), Metro, with I Speak Machine 18 September – Toronto, ON (Canada), Phoenix Concert Theatre, with I Speak Machine 19 September – Montreal, QC (Canada), SAT, with I Speak Machine 21 September – Boston, MA (US), The Wilbur, with I Speak Machine 25 September – New York, NY (US), Knockdown Center, with I Speak Machine 26 September – Philadelphia, PA (US), Underground Arts, with I Speak Machine 7 October – Dublin (Ireland), The Academy 8 October – Belfast (UK), Limelight 10 October – Birmingham (UK), Town Hall, with Gazelle Twin 11 October – Liverpool (UK), Arts Club, with Gazelle Twin 13 October – Nottingham (UK), The Palais, with Gazelle Twin 14 October – Cardiff (UK), The Globe, with Fader 15 October – Bath (UK), Forum, with Fader 17 October – Newcastle (UK), Boiler Shop, with Gazelle Twin 18 October – Glasgow (UK), Barrowland, with Gazelle Twin 19 October – Manchester (UK), Albert Hall, with Gazelle Twin 21 October – Brighton (UK), Chalk, with Gazelle Twin 22 October – London (UK), Roundhouse, with Gazelle Twin 25 October – Sheffield (UK), Octagon, with Gazelle Twin – sold out About Cabaret Voltaire Cabaret Voltaire formed in Sheffield in 1973 around Richard H. Kirk, Stephen Mallinder and Chris Watson, working with tape manipulation, electronics and found sound well before the equipment caught up with the idea. Watson left in 1981. Kirk and Mallinder continued as a duo, signing to EMI in the mid-1980s and issuing “CODE” in 1987, the album that produced their two UK chart singles, “Don’t Argue” and “Here To Go”. The pair wound the project down in 1994. Kirk later carried the name alone, performing at Berlin’s Atonal festival in 2014 and issuing the connected run of “Shadow of Fear”, “BN9Drone” and “Dekadrone” across 2020 and 2021. He died in autumn 2021. Mallinder and Watson returned to the stage in 2025 to mark 50 years since the band’s first performance, a run that included a Roundhouse booking for 2026 and continued into this year around the live album “But What Time Is It Really?”, from which the pair also shared a live “Yashar”. The “CODE” reissue lands three weeks into that final tour.

items.body: Belgian cold wave and EBM duo Parade Ground put their 1988 debut album “Cut Up” back on vinyl on 4 September through VUZ Records, in three 180-gram colour pressings of 100 copies each: clear glass, clear orange and clear orange smoke. Each carries a lyrics inlay. The same day brings two pressings of the companion album “Remixes”, on smoked grey and opaque white, again limited to 100 copies apiece. Cut Up by Parade Ground “Cut Up” was the first full-length from brothers Jean-Marc and Pierre Pauly, originally issued by PIAS. The record was cut at A.B.S. Studio in Brussels, with the exception of “Moans”, recorded at Daylight Studio and produced by Wire‘s Colin Newman, who also plays guitar and synthesizer and sings backing vocals on it. Jean-Marc Pauly handles vocals, guitar and keyboard, Pierre Pauly bass, keyboards, percussion and backing vocals. Daniel Caron wrote the music for “Cut Up The Neck-Tie”. The nine tracks run “Hollywood”, “Modern Hunting”, “I Will Talk”, “Moans”, “Moist Hands”, “Such Is The Bow”, “Cut Up The Neck-Tie”, “Cut-Throat Business” and “Strange World”. The album sits close to the Belgian electronic scene that produced Front 242, with whose members the brothers kept working ties, but its combination of stark electronics, post-punk guitar and studio experiment stayed its own thing. Parade Ground’s ‘Remixes’ collects eight Peter Rainman reworks The “Remixes” LP gathers eight tracks from across the back catalogue reworked by French producer Peter Rainman, who records as People Theatre and has remixed for Apoptygma Berzerk, Chinese Theatre and Psyche. Rather than take the originals apart, Rainman keeps their arrangements and atmosphere and adds new textures and rhythms. The running order is “Moan on the Sly (People Theatre’s Catch Mix)”, “The Net (People Theatre’s Vault Mix)”, “I shut My Eyes (People Theatre’s Optic Mix)”, “Took Advantage (People Theatre’s Favour Mix)”, “Gold Rush (People Theatre’s Klondike Mix)”, “A Day at the Park (People Theatre’s Footsteps Mix)”, “Retired (People Theatre’s Laugh Mix)” and “Strange World (People Theatre’s Airplane And Crash Mix)”. Side-Line covered the collection when it arrived as the second 45th anniversary release in April 2026. About Parade Ground Parade Ground started in Brussels in 1981 as a duo of brothers Jean-Marc Pauly on vocals and Pierre Pauly on bass and keyboards. A run of maxi-singles between 1983 and 1987 came before “Cut Up”, their 1988 debut album for PIAS, recorded largely at A.B.S. Studio and marked by Colin Newman’s production work on “Moans”. “The 15th Floor” followed in 1989, though it only reached CD in 2021. The brothers kept the project going in bursts: “Sanctuary” arrived in 2018 in a run of 300 copies, their first live album “Life (Live in Frankfurt)” in June 2019, and 2007’s “Rosary” returned as a download in December 2021. The 336-page book “Words Sword Words”, issued with a CD, appeared in July 2024. Jean-Marc Pauly set out the pair’s working aim in a 2019 Side-Line interview. VUZ Records has handled the recent catalogue work, from the archival compilation “Heaven With Care” in October 2025 through the 45th anniversary items of 2026: the “Strange World” 3-inch CD-R and digital edition in February and “Remixes” in April. The 4 September pressings extend that anniversary run to vinyl.

TC75)”, “Stay Away” and “Inner Resonance”. Pyrroline wrote, produced and performed the album themselves. TC75‘s Tino Claus contributes guest vocals to “Relentless”, and the lyrics of “Stay Away” draw on Dylan Thomas, James Whitcomb Riley and Lord Alfred Tennyson. Ambiguity by PYRROLINE The album follows the double CD “Struggling” by five years, and moves through transition, doubt, technological change and the effects of war. The label describes the record as combining “cold synthetic textures, driving rhythms and atmospheric soundscapes with lyrics that remain deliberately open, fragmented and tense”. About Pyrroline Pyrroline is an electro-industrial and old-school EBM duo built around Arnte on vocals and Schmoun on synths and chants. The project records for Electro Aggression Records, the label founded in 2011 that concentrates on old-school EBM and electronic body music, and has stayed with it across its full-length run. Side-Line covered the CD album “In The Dawn Of Freedom” in September 2017 and the double CD “Struggling” in May 2021, the latter the duo’s fifth album. The sixth album “Ambiguity” was announced in June 2026 and shipped the following month. “Day 45” is the latest clip taken from it.

items.body: Diary of Dreams‘s tenth studio album, “Ego:X”, turns 15 this year. The German darkwave act released the record through Accession Records on 26 August 2011 in Europe, with a US release following on 11 September 2011 via Metropolis Records. “Ego:X” arrived in four editions: a regular CD with 14 tracks, an extended digital edition with additional bonus material, a 2xLP vinyl set, and a limited deluxe box housing a two-disc set alongside a 60-page book and hand-signed cards. The album was produced by Daniel Myer together with Diary of Dreams, recorded and mastered at White Room 5, with Rainer Assmann handling mastering and Guido Fricke on pre-mastering and acoustic drum recording. Adrian Hates wrote and performed the material, backed on the album by Dejan, Flex and Gaun:A, who also contributed the painted artwork. The regular-edition tracklist runs “Into X,” “Undividable,” “Lebenslang,” “Grey the Blue,” “Element 1: Zeitgeist,” “Immerdar,” “Push Me” featuring Amelia Brightman, “Echo in Me (X-Version),” “Splinter,” “Element 5: Resignation,” “Mein-Eid,” “Fateful Decoy,” “Weh:Mut” and “Out of X.” The spoken-word narration threaded between songs was read by Martin Keßler, the German dubbing voice of Nicolas Cage and Vin Diesel. Violinist Ray W. added additional violin on “Undividable” and “Push Me.” The lead single, “Echo in Me,” was released on 12 November 2010 ahead of the album. “Ego:X” followed Diary of Dreams’ ninth album, “(if),” from March 2009, and the 2010 best-of compilation “A Collection Of…” About Diary of Dreams Diary of Dreams is a German darkwave project initiated by classically trained guitarist and pianist Adrian Hates in the late 1980s, taking its name from one of his early classical guitar compositions, “Tagebuch der Träume.” Hates had previously played guitar for Garden of Delight. The first Diary of Dreams album, “Cholymelan,” appeared in 1994 on the Dion Fortune label. Hates then founded his own label, Accession Records, which released the band’s second album, “End of Flowers,” in 1996, followed by “Bird Without Wings” in 1997 and the more experimental “Psychoma?” in 1998. The compilation “Moments of Bloom” appeared in 1999, reworking tracks from the first three albums. “One of 18 Angels” (2000) and “Freak Perfume” (2002), plus its companion EP “PaniK Manifesto,” pushed the sound toward heavier use of electronic rhythms. The 2004 concept album “Nigredo” drew on a mythology the band designed itself, and songs from its tour were later released on the live album “Alive,” which reached number 2 on the German Alternative Charts. The EP “Menschfeind” followed in 2005, and “Nekrolog 43” in 2007. The ninth album, “(if),” arrived on 13 March 2009, and the compilation “A Collection Of…” followed in March 2010. “Ego:X,” the tenth studio album, followed the November 2010 single “Echo in Me” and arrived in Europe on 26 August 2011, with the US edition released on 11 September 2011 through Metropolis Records. Diary of Dreams went on to release “Elegies in Darkness” in 2014, “Grau im Licht” in 2015, “Hell in Eden” in 2017, “Melancholin” in 2023 and “Under a Timeless Spell” in 2024, the latter covered previously on Side-Line. The band began its “Dead End Dreams” chapter series on Accession Records with Chapter 1 in September 2025. “Ego:X” marks its 15th anniversary this year.

items.body: The American duo Magic Wands—comprising Dexy Valentine (guitar, keyboards, vocals) and Chris Valentine (guitar, vocals)—have already released several notable albums and returned this spring with this six-track EP. It features three new songs alongside three familiar tracks presented in a fresh guise. Magic Wands remain true to their musical identity, carefully blending Dream-Pop with a touch of Shoegaze. The guitar remains the musical highlight, creating a distinctive, dreamy atmosphere while adding a certain zest to the songs. Synths introduce an extra melodic—and at times melancholic—touch to the overall sound. Add to this the dry snare drums reminiscent of the golden era of the 80s and Dexy’s lovely, ethereal vocals, and the result is simply superb. I was particularly impressed by the first two tracks, both of which are new material. The opening track hints at Dark-Wave, yet that dark, dreamy quality remains the band’s trademark. The familiar tracks include the former single “Sacred Mirrors” (featuring Psychedelic Furs guitarist John Ashton), a remastered version of “Wishing Well,” and a remix of “Golden” (originally from their previous album). While these are all good songs, they fall just a notch below the two opening tracks, with “Starline” standing out as my absolute favorite. Magic Wands continue to do what they do best: cool Dream-Pop. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Starline”: Starline by Magic Wands About Magic Wands Magic Wands is a dream pop duo from Los Angeles, California, formed by Dexy Valentine (guitar, keyboards, vocals) and Chris Valentine (guitar, vocals). The project started in 2007 with the single “Teenage Love”. The debut album “Aloha Moon” appeared in 2011, followed by “Jupiter” in 2015, the “Lazer Bitch” 7-inch on Cleopatra in 2016, “Abrakadabra” in 2018 and the self-released “Illuminate” in 2020. The duo moved to Metropolis Records, which issued the singles “Joy” and “Time” and the album “Switch” in 2023, followed by the remix album “Switched”. “Hide” and “Armour” came in 2024, and “Across The Water”, “Time To Dream” and the LP “Cascades” in 2025. “Wishing Well” is the duo’s six-track EP for the label.

items.body: Do you feel regret Do you even know my name… Ahead of the September 18 release of Get Mean, Boy Harsher have unveiled “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call),” the third advance single from their first new album since the 2022 film and soundtrack The Runner. The song finds Jae Matthews trying to maintain the appearance of composure while an unanswered telephone turns distance into rejection, doubt, and the humiliating fear of having been forgotten. An uneasy synth introduction quickly opens into a brisk new-wave dance beat, with a firm kick, rounded bass, bright keyboards, and clipped bursts of distorted guitar giving the track a warmer and more openly pop-minded character. Matthews sings in a heartbroken drawl that seems to drag against the arrangement’s forward motion. The contrast makes the song feel almost euphoric at first, although every melodic lift carries another reminder that the person she wants remains absent. “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)” is a song that could have occupied late-night radio in the mid-1980s, when sleek synthesizers, post-punk guitar, and bruised romanticism regularly met inside a four-minute single. Boy Harsher retain the uncanny atmosphere that has always accompanied their music, yet the unease here is romantic and immediate: the sort of private crisis that can accompany a night drive while the road continues forward with far more certainty than the relationship. The verses are built from questions sent into silence. Faith has waned, time has been lost, and Jae questions whether the person on the other end feels regret or even remembers her. The plea “Do you even know my name?” cuts deep, as recognition is now the least she expects. In response to this fear, the repeated assurance “I’m OK” increasingly resembles a rehearsed line, seemingly for the benefit of the one saying it. The official lyric video transforms that rehearsal into an analog karaoke experience. Made using vintage video gear by Los Angeles video artist Sean McGuirk and shot at PropHaus Brooklyn by Jesse Korman, it keeps the camera focused on the curved glass of an old CRT television in a dimly lit room. The screen displays a cold blue background with thick yellow letters appearing beneath rolling scan lines, bowed edges, and concentric patterns created by photographing a cathode-ray display. Its opening card resembles a selection from a home karaoke catalogue: “IN THE STYLE OF,” followed by the artist, title, and parenthetical subtitle. From that point, the lyrics move across the blue background in uppercase, with parts of each line fading, smearing, or bleaching toward white alongside the vocal cues. The abbreviations “U,” “YR,” and “N” mimic the shorthand of text messaging, yet they appear on a television from an earlier technological era. Thus, a song about failed communication is conveyed through two outdated mediums: the silent, unanswered phone and the solitary glow of a karaoke machine. McGuirk also leaves the machinery’s awkward instructions intact. Cards reading “INSTRUMENTAL BREAK” interrupt the lyrics with dry literalism, while the chorus is broken into syllabic prompts that make Matthews’ faltering reassurance available for anyone to sing. Karaoke usually transforms private listening into a social performance; here, there is no visible room, microphone, or gathering of friends. The viewer faces only the television and the uneasy invitation to inhabit the singer’s denial. The absence of performers becomes the video’s central image. Matthews is heard but never seen, much as the person she addresses exists only through the failure to make contact. The warm momentum of the music presses against the cool television light until the screen returns to its title card at the end, ready to begin the selection again. That reset gives the waiting a circular quality: another call can go unanswered, another chorus can insist that everything is fine, and the machine will remain prepared to repeat the performance. Watch the lyric video for Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call) below: Stream “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)” across digital services here. Get Mean began during a period when the continuation of Boy Harsher was far from assured. In early 2024, after years of international touring and increasingly ambitious work across music and film, Matthews and Augustus Muller ended their romantic relationship. The separation followed personal turmoil, family loss, and a creative block that left both the band and the prospect of another album uncertain. Writing resumed when Matthews took to the road, moving through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, South Florida, and points between. That unsettled geography became part of the album itself. Described as Boy Harsher’s “road album,” Get Mean was recorded across eight locations in the United States, Mexico, and Italy, gathering cellphone voice notes, environmental recordings, and changing emotional states along the way. Matthews describes the album as: “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” Across its twelve tracks, the duo’s familiar coldwave momentum meets detuned pads, abrasive synth leads, pedal-steel bends, New Romantic guitar, percussive jokes, and unadorned phone recordings. Those additions allow grief and exhaustion to coexist with flirtation, humor, and the possibility of beginning again. The album follows the collapse of one form of intimacy while testing whether another—the creative bond between Matthews and Muller—can survive it. Get Mean arrives September 18 via Atlantic Records. Pre-order and pre-save the album here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Matthews and Muller formed Boy Harsher in 2014 after meeting while studying film in Savannah. Their first EP, Lesser Man, began as a small cassette release before “Pain” spread widely online. The duo followed it with Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. Their filmmaking background came fully into view with The Runner, the 2022 horror film and accompanying soundtrack that they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their cinematic work continues with The Lonely Woman, their forthcoming feature-length horror thriller starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, Sturgill Simpson, Will Oldham, and Jake Weary. Boy Harsher are directing the film and providing its score. Following the release of Get Mean, Boy Harsher will begin an extensive North American headline tour before continuing through Europe and the United Kingdom with support from Choir Boy. The itinerary includes sold-out two-night runs in Chicago and Portland, a sold-out Los Angeles appearance at the Hollywood Palladium, and newly sold-out dates in Denver, Paris, Glasgow, and Bristol. items.body: Most fantasies of quitting preserve some faith in manners: a resignation letter, a slammed drawer, a final walk past reception. Mighty Crimes tears through that decorum with a workplace homicide and a car pointed toward open country. Yet escape does not clear the mind. The office recedes while the argument continues in the driver’s seat, where relief, panic, and self-justification take turns holding the wheel. London post-punk band Blow Dry, the project conceived and led by Sydney-born frontwoman Genevieve Welsh, have shared their off-kilter video for Mighty Crimes. Released on July 28 and co-written with Jorge Elbrecht—whose credits include Japanese Breakfast, Sky Ferreira, and Angel Olsen—the song turns an under-the-breath workplace fantasy into fugitive comedy. Sick of corporate life, a woman kills her boss, runs for the horizon, and gradually loses command of her own explanation. A spring-loaded bass line opens the track, with clipped guitar accents and post-punk jangles darting around percussion that carries the fleet, slightly camp momentum of a 1960s heist score. An eerie rising-and-falling figure, poised somewhere between an organ buzz and a guitar whine, keeps the floor tilted beneath Welsh’s theatrical delivery. Her voice purrs, quivers, yelps, and steadily pushes toward the edge as each repetition makes the character sound less convinced by her own defence. Welsh explains: “On the surface it’s a relatable laugh – ugh, I want to kill my boss – I mean, how many people have said that before?! But there are real emotions under the humour too: the freedom and release of throwing everything away and heading out into the unknown, tangled up with the anxiety of ‘what have I done,’ and then comes the self-talk you do to convince yourself that yes you were right to make the choices you’ve made… whether you actually were or not. Or at least, that’s the mental olympics my brain goes through. It’s such a playful track combined with the Blow Dry dark humour – as soon as we recorded it I could see the imagery – a Thelma & Louise meets Tarantino meets Priscilla, Queen of the Desert getaway film, but set in the Australian outback. An off-kilter homage to my homeland.” Speaking with Eliot Odgers for Still Listening Magazine, Welsh said that writing through a fictional character “let me detach and have more fun.” The small crew followed a similar instinct while filming in Western Australia: “No permissions, a rough plan, and the rest we were winging.” Directed by Blair Gauld, with cinematography by Ryan Murphy and grading by Spike Luke Wright, the video carries the song’s office-crime premise into the red vastness surrounding Kalgoorlie. Welsh’s outlaw stands against burnt-orange earth and an immense blue sky, her white clothing and wind-tossed hair cutting across the Goldfields landscape. The Coolgardie Caravan Park and Broad Arrow Tavern anchor the getaway in a specific corner of Western Australia. Meat pies, a Bunnings hat, skimpy-bar culture, and other slices of Australiana bring homesick affection and dry comedy to the flight. With only three people travelling and filming, the clip retains the looseness of its production: a desert crime picture assembled through roadside encounters, local generosity, and the willingness to see what might happen next. Watch the video for Mighty Crimes below: Blow Dry brings Welsh’s background in fashion and love of cinema into a theatrical strain of post-punk informed by punk rock, new wave, and gothic rock. The group’s recent single MR. BIG introduced its more confrontational side through an aggressive, dance-led performance video; Mighty Crimes widens the frame into character-driven film and black comedy. Alongside stylist Matt King, Welsh also runs Tainted Pleasure, a Blitz Club-inspired night held at The Social in London. Mighty Crimes is out now. Listen on Spotify and Apple Music. items.body: I am sitting in the darkStaring at nothingCaged by the shadows I become rottenMy emotions go to another stageEscape from this cave Plato’s allegory of the cave begins with one of philosophy’s most unsettling propositions: human beings may spend their lives confusing appearances for reality. His prisoners, chained underground since childhood, know the world through forms projected across stone. To encounter the world beyond their enclosure would require a painful revision of everything they believed to be true. Knowledge, in this conception, begins with the terrifying possibility that the mind has mistaken confinement for the universe. Berlin-based Brazilian artist Daniel Knutz brings that ancient problem inward on The Cave, turning Plato’s cavern into an enclosure built from memory, fear, exhaustion, and emotional paralysis. The walls possess their own acoustics. Thoughts return altered by repetition; tears strike stone; a heartbeat seems to travel through chambers where time has become difficult to measure. Knutz presents consciousness as something almost geological, with experience deposited layer upon layer until the past acquires the weight of rock. Musically, The Cave belongs to the grander tradition of darkwave and gothic rock represented by Clan of Xymox, Fields of the Nephilim, Danse Society, and London After Midnight. There is breadth in its atmosphere and a sense of scale suited to Knutz’s subject. The production treats space as an instrument: distant sounds, cavernous resonance, and deliberate repetition make the listener aware of imagined dimensions beyond the speakers. It feels less like observing someone’s isolation than occupying its architecture. Memory is rarely an archive from which we retrieve pristine records. Each recollection passes once more through the mind that remembers it, altered by present fear, desire, guilt, and age. Knutz’s cave therefore becomes an enormous resonating chamber in which consciousness continually encounters itself. “The Cave is a journey into the depths of my own mind,” says Knutz. “The cave symbolizes the hidden places within us where memories echo, fears grow, and emotions remain trapped in darkness. The atmosphere of the song is shaped by the sounds of the cave itself: distant echoes, dripping water, and tears falling onto stone. These sounds represent memories and emotions repeating through time, creating a feeling of isolation and reflection. Even the heartbeat feels as if it is resonating through the cold walls, emphasizing the loneliness and weight of the moment.” The accompanying video, conceived and directed by Streykatt, extends this idea into mountains and an underground cavern rendered in drained, earthen tones. Knutz moves through terrain that seems older than individual suffering, reducing one person’s crisis against the immense scale of stone and geological time. The imagery gives his solitude a strange, almost prehistoric quality. Watch the video for The Cave below: Yet Plato’s prisoners were offered the possibility of ascent. Daniel Knutz leaves that possibility painfully open: self-knowledge as illumination is earned through confrontation, when the mind finally recognizes the walls surrounding it. Somewhere beyond the cold stone, another conception of the self remains possible. The first evidence of freedom may simply be realizing that the cave has an exit. The cave is included on Daniel Knutz’s latest album, Echoes. Listen to The Cave below and order the album here. items.body: You know it felt like a war, hungover on a parquet floor But now it’s like I hardly think about you anymore Adulthood is an exercise in presentation. We learn the correct expressions and develop plausible explanations for why the compromises we once feared are now signs of wisdom. On Desperate Journalist‘s Terrible Years, the lead single from the London quartet’s sixth album, Gilding the Lily, lead singer Jo Bevan turns that performance into a social comedy, complete with escape, panic, and the suspicion that maturity may simply be youth with better excuses. The song begins with Rob Hardy’s verse progression and expands into three minutes of crowded guitars, orchestral synths, and a rhythm section that keeps pressing forward as though hesitation might expose somebody. Simon Drowner’s bass and Caz Helbert’s drums give the track an eager gait, while Hardy’s guitar has the bright edge and density that made Desperate Journalist recognizable. After the sparse, industrial cast of No Hero, the arrangement feels luxuriant and busy, capped by a chiming middle eight whose sweetness sharpens the song’s mockery rather than softening it. “This is one of the last songs we wrote for the album,” Bevan explains. “Rob had a kernel of an idea for the verse chord progression and we all goaded him into basically writing all the rest of the music one day at rehearsal. Lyrically it’s from the perspective of a character who’s cashed in and moved to LA or somewhere exotic, and is mistakenly under the impression that they are now blissfully balanced (and definitely not in denial about how much they miss the chaos and excitement of their youth). It’s sort of sympathetic but also caustic, as they’re lording it over the people they used to know whilst still clearly being a bit of a mess and scared of how old they’ve become. A lot of this album is about the horror of becoming aware of your own mortality – but, you know, in a fun way.” Bevan sings from inside a personality built to advertise success, allowing vanity and fear to occupy the same immaculate room. The character has escaped, cashed in, moved somewhere sunny, and achieved the balance everyone else failed to find. Yet every boast carries the faint desperation of a holiday photograph posted for an audience of former friends. Jez Leather’s performance video, filmed with warm lights in a white room, gives the song an uncluttered frame. The band plays with a directness that suits its raucous construction, leaving Bevan’s words to supply the psychological mess. Watch the video for Terrible Years below: Desperate Journalist are a London post-punk quartet comprising vocalist Jo Bevan, guitarist Rob Hardy, bassist Simon Drowner, and drummer Caz Helbert. Across five albums, the band have paired richly layered guitars and propulsive rhythms with Bevan’s incisive lyrics, gradually incorporating the electronic and industrial textures heard on 2024’s No Hero. Their forthcoming sixth album, Gilding the Lily, continues that evolution while preserving the melodic force and emotional candor at the heart of their work. As an introduction to Gilding the Lily, due out on November 20 through Fierce Panda Records, Terrible Years suggests Desperate Journalist are fascinated by the humiliations hidden inside self-possession: the older we become, the more elaborate our methods for pretending we have arrived. items.body: There are places on Earth that seem to contain more world than geography should permit. A shoreline at dusk, an abandoned road, a drowned foundation beneath still water: each can suggest that reality possesses hidden rooms, inaccessible except through attention. On Illusion of an Inland Ocean, due October 30, Eric Angelo Bessel makes music for that suspicion, eighteen connected compositions in which ordinary terrain seems to open upon immensities. Based in Portland, Oregon, Bessel works at the intersection of memory, landscape, and technology, subjects united by their peculiar relationship with time. His music, photography, and design all share an interest in the traces people and places leave behind: evidence that something existed, changed, disappeared, or continues beyond immediate perception. Across his various disciplines, he seems less interested in documenting the world as it appears than in examining how perception alters it, and how memory can transform a place into something larger, stranger, and almost limitless. The first single, Pathways, released on August 25, offers an ideal entry point. Its patient, ambient movement recalls The Caretaker, William Basinski, Loscil, Stars of the Lid, and Faten Kanaan, yet Bessel approaches that lineage with a distinct sense of terrestrial mystery. The music feels cinematic and powerful because it enlarges perception. A familiar landscape begins to seem ancient; a road becomes a coordinate; water becomes an archive. Tiny details acquire the gravity of astronomical objects viewed from a distance. Mellotrons, guitars, and layers of analogue processing become instruments of gradual revelation, with tones accumulating, dissolving, and returning in altered forms. Melody seems to come into focus by degrees, as though perceived across a great distance, while small shifts in texture can change the apparent dimensions of the entire piece. The music encourages sustained attention rather than movement toward some final point, rewarding repeated listening with connections that may have remained invisible before. Its accompanying visualizer deepens that sensation by placing us underwater, where life passes through channels of static and unstable transmission. The images suggest cameras lowered into a region beyond human access, recording organisms, currents, and possible thresholds that our senses were never designed to comprehend. The ocean has always possessed this cosmic quality. We know its presence intimately, yet portions of it remain unseen, populated by forms of life so remote from daily experience that they can seem almost extraterrestrial. Watch the video for Pathways below: Written, recorded, mixed, and produced entirely by Bessel, Illusion of an Inland Ocean is expansive without becoming crowded. Tones gather slowly, suspended in spaces, while distant textures seem to recede beyond the edge of hearing. There is a frequency of peace running through the record, though serenity here is never simple. Silence becomes evidence, a faint indication that something vast continues beyond the narrow bandwidth of human awareness. Beneath it lies the awareness that the universe, and even our planet, remains filled with regions we cannot completely know. Composed in the pale hours of early morning and refined deep into the night, the album occupies that uncertain territory where dreams, memory, and observation begin to lose their boundaries. Bessel has long been drawn to these transitional states, when the mind has loosened its allegiance to ordinary time and the familiar world can suddenly appear immense, remote, or newly discovered. Bessel treats mystery as a condition of existence rather than a puzzle awaiting solution. The album asks for stillness, the kind that precedes sleep, when the architecture of the waking world loosens and distances become difficult to measure. Listening then can feel like drifting beyond the mapped edge of experience, not toward fantasy so much as toward a heightened awareness of how little we perceive. In that sense, Bessel has made an album about scale: the immense concealed inside the commonplace, the unknown beneath our feet, and the quiet possibility that every familiar place contains a portal to somewhere we have never been. Listen to Pathways below and pre-order Illusion of an Inland Ocean here. items.body: “The silence of the Donetsk steppe is deceptive. Amid complete stillness, you begin to hear a powerful symphony rising from deep beneath the earth.” One should be careful not to romanticise the Donbas. It has never been an easy place to live. As Stanislav Aseyev writes in In Isolation, “The majority of the Donbas population is made up of working-class people who tumble out of factory gates after a 12-hour shift,” while the region itself has long oscillated between industrial pride, political manipulation and violence. “The steppe went on forever, rolling all the way to the horizon, breaking against the sky. It was an ocean of grass, shifting under the wind, smelling of dust and dry earth, immense and completely free,” writes Serhyi Zhadan in Voroshilovgrad. The landscape may appear vast and open, but beneath it lies a history shaped by coal seams, explosions, exploitation and, more recently, war. Donbas in Memoriam never loses sight of that complexity. The opening begins almost imperceptibly. There is the crackle of what sounds like electrical discharge or high-voltage leakage before the music settles into a calm ambient landscape built from synthesisers and water recordings that initially recall vintage library music. Over this appears the voice of a Soviet documentary narrator describing the Komsomolets Donbassa mine as “a ship from the future, resting upon the frozen, gigantic waves of an ancient sea.” For a brief moment one might think the piece is heading towards a conventional documentary. It does not. Gradually the soundscape mutates. Distortion begins to infiltrate the texture. Resonances accumulate. Electronic circuitry slowly consumes the archive until the narrator and successive generations of television reports, political speeches, miners’ conversations, church services and news bulletins lose their privileged position. Language is no longer the protagonist. It becomes another sonic material, absorbed into an increasingly dense acoustic geology. The transformation happens without dramatic editing or sudden contrasts, the composition growing denser almost imperceptibly as spectral layers accumulate. Intensity has little to do with volume: voices occupy familiar speech frequencies while tape hiss, industrial rumble, degraded broadcasts and electronic drones gradually crowd the space around them. By the final third of the thirty-minute work, individual testimonies have become difficult to follow, subsumed into something larger until it feels as though history itself is collapsing into sound. The effect is powerful as the archive refuses simplistic narratives. Soviet triumphalism sits alongside reports of methane explosions. Celebrations of mining records are followed by desperate appeals from families waiting outside collapsed shafts. The promises of politicians dissolve into accusations of “Liar.” Everyday conversations about fishing coexist with artillery, church kitchens and humanitarian aid. Rather than imposing a historical argument, Muzychna Shkatulka allows contradictory voices to remain unresolved. This refusal to simplify is perhaps the album’s greatest strength. As John McDonnell – shadow chancellor during the Corbin leadership – has argued, the Donbas cannot be reduced to geopolitical abstractions. Behind every discussion about territory lies the lived reality of miners, trade unionists and ordinary families whose lives have been shaped by forces largely beyond their control. Likewise, Aseyev reminds us that understanding the region requires acknowledging its difficult social history rather than projecting romantic myths onto it. Donbas in Memoriam shares that honesty. It neither sentimentalises the Donbas nor transforms it into an ideological symbol. It simply listens. The second track, “Improv”, performs a very different function. Built around persistent low-frequency vibration, the piece feels almost geological from the outset. Here memory seems to emerge from the landscape itself, without the archival voices of the preceding track. The music increases in density before opening up around its midpoint, only to thicken once again as resonances accumulate across the spectrum. Tension develops through the occupation of acoustic space, each gesture leaving behind a residue that colours those that follow. The subterranean pressure of the lower frequencies suggests not only the mines beneath the Donbas but also the geological history of the region. Taken together, the two works complement one another. If the title piece excavates the historical archive, “Improv” excavates the acoustic memory of the landscape itself. One speaks through voices; the other through vibration. Like the stark image of the Komsomolets Donbassa headframe on the cover, the EP transforms industrial infrastructure into a memorial without aestheticising either labour or destruction. Instead, it reminds us that landscapes remember. The voices may eventually dissolve into noise, but the resonance remains. As the poet Lyubov Yakymchuk wrote, “We will build another [home] in an apricot tree out of luscious clouds, out of azure ether.” To delve deeper into the making of Donbas in Memoriam, we reconnected with Muzychna Shkatulka after having first spoken to him for the June episode of Ukrainian Field Notes. In our previous conversation about Події, you explained that your music deliberately resisted storytelling. You even said that the pieces “mean nothing” in the sense that they do not communicate a lesson or an opinion, but simply exist as sound. Donbas in Memoriam seems to move in the opposite direction, drawing on Soviet documentaries, television broadcasts, political speeches, miners’ testimonies and everyday conversations. Yet, as the piece unfolds, these voices gradually lose their semantic function and become part of the musical texture. Did working with documentary archives change your relationship with narrative, or were you still pursuing the same idea of listening to sound before meaning? Well, in fact, the first draft of Donbas in Memoriam had been in the works since 2023; back then, it was called Комсомолець Донбасу у Пеклі [Komsomol member of Donbas in Hell] and was fully composed by me, with no use of samples or archives. At the time, I thought of it as some kind of retelling of The Divine Comedy, but I wasn’t pleased with the results and decided to postpone it until I knew what to do with it. The original Divine Comedy plan felt stupid and insincere. The only thing that survived from the original composition is the cover of “Спят курганы темные” [“Dark mounds are sleeping”—a famous Soviet lyrical song about Donbas miners, written in 1944 by composer Nikita Bogoroditsky and poet Boris Ladogin] at the end, and all the narrative elements of D.I.M. are somewhat connected to this first version. Time passed, my views on music evolved, and I decided to return to this project in the spring of 2026 while finishing the previous two releases. I don’t think that D.I.M. relies much on narrative, but of course, when talking about such a serious subject, I wanted my message to be clear and coherent. This release is more than sound to me; it is the only remaining way for me to return to my “home.” The title track begins with what sounds like an electrical discharge before opening into what feels like serene library or soundtrack music. The first archival voice describes the Komsomolets Donbassa mine as “a ship from the future,” but that optimistic vision is slowly overtaken by distortion, overlapping broadcasts and increasingly unstable sonic layers. The piece never announces a dramatic turning point; history seems to accumulate almost imperceptibly until language itself begins to dissolve. How consciously did you shape that gradual transformation, and were you thinking in musical terms, historical terms, or both at the same time? I think this gradual descent into noise is reminiscent of my own relationship with Donbas. At first, it was this kind of magical place stuck in time after the ’90s and the collapse of the USSR; Komsomolets really felt like the beating heart of my hometown and the towns nearby—not specifically “a ship from the future,” but something close. I was a kid and didn’t notice the realities of life there—the miners’ strikes, the corrupt government, the financial crisis and its impact on the working class. The one thing I remember as clear as day is playing with toys in my room and then noticing a column of smoke rising into the sky—it was the Boeing 777 crash in Torez. After that came years in exile, with news broadcasts about the slow takeover by occupying forces of the land that was once my home. Slowly, I started to understand that Donbas wasn’t really what I had imagined it to be, and that feeling is also present in the final audio work. You grew up in the Donetsk Oblast, and throughout our conversations you’ve often spoken about perception rather than memory. Listening to Donbas in Memoriam, I was struck by the fact that Donbas is neither romanticised nor reduced to a symbol of war. Instead, it emerges as a place where Soviet industrial ambition, miners’ everyday lives, political violence and geological time all coexist. Was it important for you to resist the tendency to turn Donbas into either a nostalgic lost homeland or simply a battlefield, and instead preserve its contradictions? Yes, it was really important. As much as I love fiction in art, I just can’t stand anything overdramatic or pretentious. I’ve had all the time in the world to make sense of what Donbas really is. When talking about this release with Zakhar [Zakhar Tovstoluzkyi who plays drums on the intro and main part], he said that he had always thought that “Donbas has an immaculate vibe for scary stuff.” I, of course, get it—the mythology of eastern Ukraine, and the Donbas region in particular, is full of chthonic symbols and dehumanising imagery. Even the first line on this release says, “The silence of the Donetsk Steppe is deceptive…” (just a totally normal romantic phrase about the nature of the steppe). But for me, it is also a place of comfort. So I tried to split the music evenly between my personal, nostalgic view of the region and the truth of what it became over the years. I wish I could say that it was only russia’s and Yanukovych’s fault that Donbas ended up under occupation, but I personally knew people who voluntarily supported the DPR and the armed takeover of mines. It was hard to realise that the source of this evil lay much further back in time than 2013, or even 1991. The second piece, “Improv”, feels almost as though the archive has been buried underground. Human voices disappear, replaced by low-frequency vibrations, distortion, sonic assault and immense, slowly shifting sonic masses that seem to echo the geological instability of Donbas itself. Was the idea always to balance the documentary dimension of the title track with something more elemental, allowing the landscape to speak through sound rather than through recorded testimony? No, it happened suddenly one evening while I was working on the D.I.M. title track. I was getting more and more frustrated with it, so I closed the project and improvised this piece in one take, enhancing it with effects afterwards. I would say that the title track functions as a journey through the history of the region; it reaches places I never could and tries to tie it all together with present-day reality. Because of that, “Improv” operates purely through my memories and is functionally powerless; there are no words or personalities, no facts or concrete dates. It’s all just a mash of memories and feelings that had been accumulating unresolved for years. And I don’t think this music resolves them either. Since writing this review and conducting the interview, the second track, “Improv”, has been removed from the album, although it appeared on the original release. (Gianmarco Del Re)
